note: What a given name is said to come from, as sources give it: competing explanations, each in our own words with the page that carries it. Written through scripts/name_meanings.py (merge from checked research patches); never a single confident answer where sources differ, never anything about a person. Wikipedia and Wiktionary text is CC BY-SA and is paraphrased, never pasted.

meanings.claim: In Slavic usage the name is taken from Old Church Slavonic, where it was the name of a Bulgarian ruler; behind that it is said to be of Bulgar origin, via a Medieval Greek form Bogoris. The dictionary says the meaning is not known.

sources.quote: Ultimately with unclear Bulgar origin, and with unknown meaning.
is a male name of Bulgar origin

meanings.note: The Bulgar language is poorly attested, so any single gloss for the name should be treated with care.

meanings.claim: A rival explanation is that Boris is a short form of the Slavic compound name Borislav, rather than a Bulgar word.

sources.quote: Another theory derives the name from the abbreviation of Old Church Slavonic

meanings.claim: Some reference listings give a string of glosses for the name (wolf, short, snow leopard, and 'famous battle' by way of Borislav), without saying which is supported; treat these as unresolved guesses, not findings.

sources.quote: Wolf, Short, Snow Leopard, Famous Battle (Borislav) or Fame-Bright (Robert)

meanings.claim: In Hungarian the spelling Boris has a different origin: it is a shortened pet form of the female name Borbala.

sources.quote: Clipping and -is diminutive of Borbála.

meanings.note: In a Hungarian record, Boris may be a woman's name; check the context before assuming the Slavic name.

meanings.claim: A recent English coinage from the early twentieth century, possibly made by blending Cherie or Cherry with the older name Beryl.

sources.quote: Coined in the early 20th century
possibly a blend of Cherie or Cherry and Beryl

meanings.note: The name is described as a modern coinage, so it is not an old register name.

meanings.claim: A second account joins Beryl to the prefix Cher-, from French chérie ('darling').

sources.quote: The name might have originated as a combination of the name Beryl

meanings.claim: A third account treats Cheryl as a variant of Charles, since that name is pronounced roughly 'sharl' in French.

sources.quote: The name has also been considered a variant of Charles

meanings.claim: A Slavic compound of the verb tomiti (to torture, to oppress, with softer senses such as to languish or to long for) and slava, 'glory'.

sources.quote: from Proto-Slavic *tomiti
considered to be a compound of Proto-Slavic

meanings.note: Dictionaries gloss the first element differently (torture, torment, languish, yearn), so the sense of the whole name is not fixed.

meanings.claim: Italian Giovanni descends from Latin Ioannes, which was taken from the Greek Ioannes, which in turn renders the Biblical Hebrew name Yohanan, glossed as 'God is gracious' and possibly a contraction of a longer name containing the divine name.

sources.quote: Inherited from Latin Iōannēs.
from Koine Greek Ἰωάννης (Iōánnēs), from Biblical Hebrew
Inherited from Old Church Slavonic Їѡанъ (Iōanŭ), from Ancient Greek

meanings.note: The same Hebrew name also reached Slavic languages (Ivan, via Old Church Slavonic and Greek) and Germanic ones (Johann, Johannes, Hans), so the family holds Slavic and Germanic forms of one name alongside the Italian one.

meanings.claim: Taken from the Greek name Hagne, formed on the adjective hagnos, 'pure, chaste'. It shares its source with Inez.

sources.quote: Borrowed from Ancient Greek Ἁγνή (Hagnḗ)
Doublet of Inez.

meanings.claim: In the Latin-speaking West the name was linked by popular association to Latin agnus, 'lamb'; the dictionary calls this a folk etymology, not the origin.

sources.quote: by folk etymology associated with Latin agnus

meanings.note: Do not read 'lamb' into a record as the meaning the parents meant.

meanings.claim: From Latin nives, the plural of nix, 'snow'. It comes from the Marian title Sancta Maria ad Nives, 'Our Lady of the Snows', so it is a devotional name rather than one made from a word for snow.

sources.quote: originating from Latin nivēs, the accusative plural of nix 'snow'
Sancta Maria ad Nives 'Our Lady of the Snows'

meanings.note: The source calls it an Italian name; it is also used in Croatian-speaking areas, but no separate Croatian origin was found. Spanish Nieves has the same source.

meanings.claim: A Germanic two-part name made from hadu ('battle, combat') and wig ('fight, duel'), reaching modern German as Hedwig from Old High German forms such as Haduwig.

sources.quote: a Germanic name consisting of the two elements hadu

meanings.claim: Early variant forms suggest the name may be a merger of two separate older names, one ending in 'fight' and the other in a word meaning 'hallowed'.

sources.quote: the name is the result of a conflation of two separate names

meanings.note: The page notes that variant forms (such as Hadiwih and Hadewi) are what suggest the merger.

meanings.claim: Italian Michele is the form of Michael, from Biblical Hebrew Mikha'el, read as a question: 'who is like God?'. It passed through Greek and Latin on the way.

sources.quote: Biblical Hebrew מִיכָאֵל (mîḵāʾēl, literally
Borrowed from Koine Greek Μῐχᾱήλ (Mĭkhāḗl), borrowed from Biblical Hebrew

meanings.note: In Italian Michele is a man's name; the same spelling (or Michèle) in English and French can be a form of the women's name Michelle.

meanings.claim: One explanation takes the Greek name Aikaterine from the goddess Hecate (Hekate). The dictionary notes the Oxford Dictionary of First Names finds this unconvincing.

sources.quote: Often said to be from Ἑκάτη (Hekátē
of debated meaning, possibly from ἑκάτερος

meanings.claim: Another explanation builds it from Greek hekateros ('each of the two') plus the suffix -ine, with the first sound reconstructed as Hekaterine.

sources.quote: from ἑκάτερος (hekáteros, “each of the two”)

meanings.claim: From early times the name was connected by folk etymology with Greek katharos, 'pure'. This changed the later spelling (the 'th' and, in Latin, forms such as Catharina and Katerina) but is not given as the real origin.

sources.quote: An early folk etymology to καθαρός
a common Greek-language origin of uncertain meaning

meanings.note: Italian Caterina, Catalina, Katharina, Katerina and Ekaterina are all one name; do not treat the 'pure' reading as settled.

meanings.claim: Italian form of Elizabeth: the Greek Elisabet, which transliterates the Biblical Hebrew name Elisheva, glossed 'my God is an oath'.

sources.quote: Borrowed from Ancient Greek Ἐλισάβετ (Elisábet), a transliteration of
a transliteration of the Old Testament Biblical Hebrew

meanings.note: Isabella, Isabel and Elisheba are forms of the same name, so searches for one may need the others.

meanings.claim: Giuseppe is the Italian form of Joseph. It descends from Latin, which took it from Greek, which in turn took it from the Biblical Hebrew name Yosef, glossed as '(God) shall add'.

sources.quote: Inherited from Latin
ultimately from Biblical Hebrew
(God) shall add

meanings.note: English Joseph is listed by Wiktionary as a doublet of Yusuf, so Giuseppe and Yusuf are the same name reached by different routes.

meanings.claim: Francesco comes from Medieval Latin Franciscus, an adjective-like form built on Francia (the land of the Franks) with the suffix -iscus. Francia and the Franks' name are in turn traced to a Germanic word, given by Wiktionary as meaning 'javelin'. In medieval Italian the name was glossed 'Frenchman', which is the 'Frenchman' route.

sources.quote: ultimately derived from Proto-Germanic
From Francia + -iscus
Frenchman

meanings.note: Both Wiktionary entries read the name as 'of the Franks / of Francia'; the 'Frenchman' gloss is a medieval Italian meaning of the name.

meanings.claim: A second view treats the name as having 'relatively unclear origins' and as thought to mean 'free' or 'free man'. This is offered as a thought-to-mean reading, not a settled derivation, and it runs alongside the 'Frenchman' reading.

sources.quote: has relatively unclear origins but is thought to mean

meanings.note: Wikipedia lists 'Free man', 'Frank' and 'Frenchman' together as medieval Italian glosses of Francesco, so the two readings are not exclusive in practice.

meanings.claim: Paolo is the Italian form of Latin Paulus, a Roman family name that comes from an ordinary Latin adjective meaning 'small', 'humble' or 'little'.

sources.quote: From Latin Paulus.
It derives from the Roman family name Paulus or Paullus
from the Latin adjective meaning

meanings.note: English Paul and Italian Paolo are doublets, and Portuguese Paulo / Spanish Pablo are the same name.

meanings.claim: Pietro is the Italian form of Latin Petrus, which comes from Greek Petros, 'stone, rock'. The Italian ordinary word for stone, pietra, is related to the same Greek word.

sources.quote: Inherited from Latin Petrus
compare pietra

meanings.note: Pietro is the same name as English Peter.

meanings.claim: Wikipedia describes Greek Petros as a masculine form coined from petra ('rock'), used as a translation of the Aramaic word Kefa, 'stone, rock'. On this account the name began as a rendering of an Aramaic word rather than as an old Greek personal name.

sources.quote: an invented, masculine form of Greek
was a translation of Aramaic

meanings.claim: Maria is the Latin form of the Greek Maria / Mariam, which comes from the post-Biblical Hebrew and Aramaic Maryam (Miryam). Wiktionary calls the meaning of the Hebrew uncertain, and says it has been debated for centuries; the explanations below are the ones sources give.

sources.quote: of uncertain meaning
from post-Biblical Hebrew and Aramaic
has been debated for centuries

meanings.note: Whichever explanation a source prefers, do not treat any one as established.

meanings.claim: One explanation takes the name from an Egyptian root meaning 'love, beloved'. Wikipedia describes this as the likely derivation.

sources.quote: it is likely derivative of the root

meanings.note: Other sources on the same page give Hebrew readings instead.

meanings.claim: Another explanation reads the name through Hebrew as 'bitter' (the root also seen in myrrh); Wiktionary's Miriam entry glosses Maryam as 'bitter'. A further set of readings derives it from a root meaning 'rebellion', 'mutiny' or 'disobedience'.

sources.quote: The name Mary was early etymologized as containing the Hebrew root
Some other explanations are mutiny / rebellion / disobedience from a root

meanings.claim: The popular reading 'star of the sea' (stella maris) is traced to a scribal error: an older rendering as 'drop of the sea' (stilla maris) was miscopied. It is not a derivation of the Hebrew.

sources.quote: drop of the sea
due to scribal error

meanings.note: Often repeated on name sites as the meaning of Maria; it is a later reinterpretation.

meanings.claim: Anna is the Latin and Greek form of the Biblical Hebrew name Hannah, understood as 'grace, gracious'. English Anna, Anne and Hannah are doublets of one name.

sources.quote: From Latin Anna, from Ancient Greek
from Biblical Hebrew
grace, gracious

meanings.note: The English entry notes that the form spread chiefly with devotion to St Anne, the traditional mother of Mary; this is a spread fact, not a second origin.

meanings.claim: Stefano is the Italian form of Latin Stephanus, from Greek Stephanos, a word meaning 'wreath, crown' and by extension 'reward, honour'. The Greek word comes from a verb meaning 'to encircle, to wreathe'.

sources.quote: From Latin Stephanus, from Ancient Greek
is derived from Greek
from the verb

meanings.note: Stefano is the Italian counterpart of English Stephen.

meanings.claim: Matteo is the Italian form of Latin Matthaeus, from Greek Matthaios, ultimately from the Hebrew name Mattityahu, literally 'gift of the Lord'.

sources.quote: From Latin Matthaeus, from Ancient Greek
gift of the Lord

meanings.note: Wikipedia says the Greek Matthaios replaced an earlier Greek rendering, Mattathias, of the same Hebrew name.

meanings.claim: Wikipedia gives the meaning as 'Gift of God' and describes the Hebrew name as first transliterated into Greek as Mattathias and later superseded by Matthaios, which became Matthew.

sources.quote: transliterated into Greek as
superseded by

meanings.note: Same derivation as above, with a slightly different English gloss.

meanings.claim: Andrea is Italian for Andrew: from Latin Andreas, from Greek Andreas, a word related to the Greek for 'man' (aner, andros) and glossed 'manly, strong and brave'.

sources.quote: From Latin Andreās, from Ancient Greek
Andrew is the English form from the Old French name Andreu
Male name is more common in Dalmatia and Istria

meanings.note: In Italian, Andrea is a man's name. In English and Spanish it is a woman's name, which Wiktionary calls a 'Latinate feminine form of Andreas and Andrew'; Wiktionary's Serbo-Croatian entry notes the male use is more common in Dalmatia and Istria, where Italian influence is stronger. Check the sex stated in the record before assuming either.

meanings.claim: Lucia is the feminine form of the Roman first name Lucius (Latin Lucia). Lucius is related to Latin lux, 'light', with an Etruscan parallel form noted by Wiktionary.

sources.quote: feminine form of the Roman praenomen
related to lūx

meanings.note: Wiktionary says English Lucia is a Latinate variant of Lucy, or borrowed from modern Italian.

meanings.claim: Wikipedia says Lucy comes from the Latin masculine name Lucius, with the meaning 'as of light', and offers a further gloss of dawn or daylight. These readings of the meaning sit on top of the lux derivation.

sources.quote: derived from the Latin masculine given name Lucius
born at dawn or daylight

meanings.note: 'Born at dawn or daylight' is a gloss Wikipedia gives for the meaning, not a documented naming custom.
